blocks.x: Hallstatt was one of the stops on our Austria trip, where we traveled through some of Austria’s most beautiful cities and lake towns. We had spent time exploring Salzburg before heading into the Salzkammergut region, and Hallstatt was our next stop on the way to Vienna.

Hallstatt is often described as one of the most beautiful lake towns in Austria. Austria has no shortage of beautiful lakeside towns, but Hallstatt is certainly one of the most famous. The village is tucked between Lake Hallstatt and the steep mountains of the Salzkammergut, with little houses built right along the water. It really does look like the postcard you have probably seen many times before. But the thing about Hallstatt is that the postcard view is only part of the experience.
Most people visit Hallstatt as a day trip. There are plenty of tours from Salzburg and Vienna, so it’s easy to spend a few hours exploring the village, taking the famous photos, and then moving on.
We decided to do something a little different and spend a night in Hallstatt.
Staying in Hallstatt

One thing you need to know if you’re driving to Hallstatt is that you can’t simply drive into the historic center and pull up in front of your hotel. The village center is closed to regular car traffic, including hotel and guesthouse guests. You’ll need to park outside the center and then make your way into town.

For overnight visitors staying in the center, there is actually a hotel parking system. Guests can use the P1 parking area and a shuttle can take them and their luggage to their accommodation, but the shuttle does not run late into the evening. The current schedule is until 7 PM.
We arrived after the shuttle had stopped running, so we ended up walking from the parking lot to our inn with all of our luggage. So this is something to keep in mind when planning your arrival.

There is also another thing to keep in mind when staying overnight: Hallstatt is a very small town, and it gets quiet early. So, once the day-trippers leave, it really slows down. Shops close early, and restaurants don’t stay open late. During our visit, we had a surprisingly difficult time finding somewhere to eat after about 8:30 or 9 PM.

So if you’re staying overnight, don’t assume you can have a late dinner whenever you feel like it. Plan dinner earlier, especially if you’re traveling with children. Hallstatt is not the kind of place where you’ll find a row of restaurants still serving dinner at 10 PM.
For us, though, the early closing was also part of the charm. Once the crowds disappeared, Hallstatt became incredibly peaceful.
Why We Stayed Overnight

We stayed at Bräugasthof, a small guesthouse right on the shore of Lake Hallstatt. The building itself has an interesting history: it dates back to the 15th century and was first documented in 1472. In 1504, it was granted brewing rights, and it remained a brewery until 1907. Today, it’s a small guesthouse and restaurant right by the lake.

There are several hotels and guesthouses along the lake, and if you’re considering staying overnight, I’d look for one right on the waterfront. It’s not necessarily about the hotel itself. It’s about being able to wake up and step out onto a balcony or terrace with the lake and mountains right in front of you.
The biggest advantage of staying overnight, though, is timing. You get to see Hallstatt before the day-trippers arrive.

In the morning, the village is still quiet. You can walk through the little streets and along the lake without the crowds that will fill them later in the day. Then, as the day-trippers start arriving, you can go off to visit the salt mine or other attractions. And in the evening, the tour groups leave. The streets empty out. The little village becomes quiet again, and you get to experience the stillness of Hallstatt after most of the visitors have gone.

We happened to be there in early August, and even though it was summer, the morning air was surprisingly crisp and refreshing. I remember stepping out in the morning and seeing the lake and mountains from our balcony. There was something incredibly peaceful about being surrounded by all that natural beauty before the day had really started.
And it happened to be my birthday. I can’t think of many better places to wake up on your birthday.
Then came breakfast.

We had breakfast right at the inn, sitting beside the lake. The lake was right in front of us, the mountains surrounding us, and the morning air still cool and fresh. It was one of those travel moments that wasn’t really an “activity” at all. We weren’t checking anything off our list. We were just sitting there, having breakfast and taking in the view. And honestly, that’s what staying overnight in Hallstatt is about for me.
A day trip lets you see Hallstatt. Staying overnight lets you experience Hallstatt—before the crowds arrive, after they leave, and in those quiet hours in between.
Explore the Old Town
There isn’t necessarily a long list of attractions you have to check off in Hallstatt. Part of the fun is simply walking through the village.

The Market Square (Marktplatz) is the center of the historic village, with colorful buildings, cafés and the Holy Trinity statue. From there, you can wander through the narrow streets toward the lakefront.
The Evangelical Church of Hallstatt is another landmark you can’t miss. Its tall, slender tower is the one you see in so many photographs of Hallstatt—including our famous viewpoint photo.

Another interesting stop is the Catholic Parish Church and the Hallstatt Charnel House, also called the Bone House. The small ossuary contains more than 600 painted skulls. It is definitely unusual and one of those things you don’t expect to find in such a pretty little lakeside village.
If you have more time, the World Heritage Museum is another option for learning about Hallstatt’s extraordinarily long history.
The Famous Hallstatt Photo Spot
Of course, we couldn’t visit Hallstatt without taking the famous Hallstatt photo.

The iconic viewpoint is officially called the Hallstatt Photo Point, also known as the Classic Village Viewpoint. This is the spot where you get the postcard view of the village, with the lake in front, the houses along the shore, the distinctive tower of the Evangelical Church, and the mountains behind them.
And yes, we took our own version of that famous photo.

What I liked about having an overnight stay was that taking this photo didn’t have to be a race. We could see the viewpoint when we wanted to, come back later, and enjoy the village at different times of the day. And the view really is as pretty in person as it is in the photographs.
Visit the Hallstatt Salt Mine
After enjoying the town, we headed up to the Hallstatt Salt Mine, officially called Salzwelten Hallstatt.
This was one of the highlights of our visit, especially because it wasn’t just a typical museum where everyone has to quietly read signs and look at old objects.
The salt mine takes you through 7,000 years of salt-mining history. You ride the funicular up the mountain, walk through the historic mining area, and then go underground into the mine itself.
And there is a fun ride inside the mine!

The miners’ slides are one of the most memorable parts of the experience. The longest one is about 64–65 meters long, so you’re not just learning about what life was like for miners—you actually get to have a little fun along the way. There’s also a mine train and an underground salt lake.
Miner’s slide inside the Salt Mine

For our family, this was a great combination of fun and informative. The kids didn’t feel like they were being dragged through another historical attraction, while we still got to learn something interesting about the history of Hallstatt.
The salt mine is also a good family activity because children as young as four can visit. Just remember that the mine itself stays around 46°F (8°C), so bring a jacket even if it’s warm outside.
Don’t Miss the Hallstatt Skywalk
The salt mine visit also gives you access to another major Hallstatt attraction: the Hallstatt Skywalk – World Heritage View.

The funicular takes you about 360 meters above the village, where the Skywalk extends out over the mountainside. From there, you get a completely different perspective of Hallstatt and Lake Hallstatt.

So if you visit the salt mine, don’t think of it as just a salt mine. The experience includes the mountain ride, the prehistoric burial grounds, the Skywalk and the spectacular views in addition to the underground mine.
More Things to Do Around Hallstatt
If you have more time than we did, there are several other things you can add to your Hallstatt-area itinerary.
Take a boat ride on Lake Hallstatt. Seeing the village from the water gives you yet another perspective of those mountains and lakeside houses.
Visit the Hallstatt Museum. It’s a good option if you want to understand more about the area’s incredibly long history.
Explore the Echern Valley (Echerntal). This is a greener, quieter side of Hallstatt with hiking trails, streams and waterfalls.

And if you have a full extra day, you can venture beyond Hallstatt itself into the surrounding Hallstatt-Dachstein-Salzkammergut region. Across the lake in Obertraun, you’ll find Dachstein Krippenstein, with attractions such as the Dachstein Ice Cave and the 5 Fingers viewing platform. Those are not actually in Hallstatt, so I’d treat them as a separate day/area rather than part of the Hallstatt village visit.
Is Hallstatt Worth Staying Overnight?
For us, yes.

If you’re short on time, Hallstatt works perfectly well as a day trip. You can see the famous view, walk around the village, visit the salt mine, and get a good feel for what makes Hallstatt so popular.
But I think the experience is very different when you stay overnight.
We weren’t rushing from one attraction to another. We had time to walk around, enjoy the lake, have breakfast right by the water, and see Hallstatt at a slower pace.

And honestly, that’s what I remember most about Hallstatt—not just the famous postcard view, but sitting by that beautiful lake with the mountains all around us and having nowhere else we needed to be. For us, it was also about those little moments in between the sightseeing. Waking up on a crisp August morning with the mountains and lake right outside our balcony. Sitting by the lake for breakfast at our inn. And, of course, doing all of that on my birthday.

Hallstatt is beautiful and absolutely worth seeing, but if you have the time, I think it’s worth giving yourself more than a few hours here. The famous postcard view is what brings you to Hallstatt, but the quiet morning and peaceful evening are what make you glad you stayed.
A day trip lets you see Hallstatt. Staying overnight lets you experience Hallstatt.
